front: What makes an account root?
back: UID 0, not the name. Root’s home directory is `/root`, and no permission check stops it. Work as a standard user and borrow root’s power one command at a time.

front: How do you tell a standard user’s prompt from root’s?
back: A root shell usually ends its prompt with `#`, a standard user’s with `$`.

front: Which UIDs do standard users have on Debian?
back: 1000 and up. Mira, as the first standard user on the machine, has UID 1000.

front: What are system users, and what UIDs do they have?
back: Accounts that belong to programs, not people, such as `www-data`. Their UIDs are below 1000 on Debian.

front: Why do system users usually have `/usr/sbin/nologin` as their shell?
back: Nobody can open an interactive session as them. They exist so that files and processes can be owned by something other than root.

front: Why does a web server run as `www-data` instead of root?
back: If the server is hacked, the attacker gets only that account’s few permissions, not root’s.

front: Which password does `sudo` ask for, and which does `su` ask for?
back: `sudo` asks for your own password. `su` asks for the password of the account you switch to, root’s if you give no name.

front: Which group lets a user run `sudo` on Debian, and which file configures it?
back: The group `sudo` on Debian and Ubuntu (`wheel` on Red Hat-family systems). The configuration is in `/etc/sudoers`.

front: What is the difference between `su jonas` and `su - jonas`?
back: `su - jonas` (or `su -l`) starts a full login shell with Jonas’s environment and home directory. Plain `su jonas` keeps most of your current environment. Leave with `exit`.

front: Why do administrators prefer `sudo` over sharing root’s password?
back: `sudo` runs a single command as root, uses each person’s own password and logs every use, so you can see who did what.

front: Which command logs Ada in to `build.tuxpixel.example`, and what does it do?
back: `ssh ada@build.tuxpixel.example`. It gives you a shell on the server over an encrypted connection; `exit` or Ctrl+D ends the session. The server listens on TCP port 22.

front: How do you use another SSH port with `ssh` and with `scp`?
back: `ssh -p 2222 host` (lower-case) and `scp -P 2222 file host:` (capital). In `scp`, lower-case `-p` means preserve times and modes.

front: Which command copies `level1.txt` to `/home/ada/` on the build server?
back: `scp level1.txt ada@build.tuxpixel.example:/home/ada/`. The remote side is the one with `host:`, and `-r` copies directories.

front: Where does ssh store the keys of servers you have connected to?
back: In `~/.ssh/known_hosts`. If a server’s key changes, ssh warns loudly, because someone might be pretending to be the server.

front: Which command creates an SSH key pair, and what are the two files called?
back: `ssh-keygen`, for example `ssh-keygen -t ed25519`. It writes the private key `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` and the public key `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub`.

front: Which SSH key may you share, and where does it go?
back: The public key. It goes on its own line in `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` of the account you log in to on the server. The private key never leaves your computer.

front: Which helper copies your public key to a server?
back: `ssh-copy-id ada@build.tuxpixel.example`. Afterwards you log in without the account password (or with the key’s passphrase, if you set one).

front: Which permissions does `sshd` expect for `~/.ssh` and `authorized_keys`?
back: Usually `700` for the directory and `600` for the file. If other users can write to them, sshd ignores the file.

front: Which command shows your UID, GID and groups?
back: `id`. It tells you whether you are root, a standard user or a system user, and which groups you belong to.

front: Which command is the safe way to edit `/etc/sudoers`?
back: `visudo`. It checks the syntax before saving. Extra rules go in small files in `/etc/sudoers.d/`.

front: What is the principle of least privilege?
back: Give each account only the rights its job needs, and borrow root with `sudo` for single commands.
